subject: geography
title: US Middle School Geography - Globalization and Trade Reading
subtitle: Reading passages about trade routes, supply chains, ports, case studies, and sustainability.
description: This reading pack gives students source-style passages and comprehension questions about globalization, supply chains, transportation, climate, labor, sustainability, and trade disruptions.

data.sourcePassage: Globalization can be seen in ordinary objects. A phone may be designed in one country, assembled in another, and made from minerals mined in several others. Sneakers can include rubber, cotton, polyester, dyes, glue, and packaging that each came from different places. Trade is one major part of this connected world. People, companies, and countries buy, sell, or exchange goods and services. Geography helps explain why trade happens because resources, climates, workers, technology, ports, and roads are not spread evenly. These connections can create jobs, choices, and access to useful products. They can also create challenges, including pollution, unsafe working conditions, dependence on distant suppliers, and pressure on natural resources.

questions.question: What is one everyday product mentioned as an example of globalization?
questions.modelAnswer: A phone or sneakers are mentioned as everyday examples of globalization.

questions.question: Which statement best describes trade?
options: Buying, selling, or exchanging goods and services
Only moving people from place to place
Refusing to use products from other places
questions.modelAnswer: Trade is buying, selling, or exchanging goods and services.

questions.question: Why does geography help explain trade?
questions.modelAnswer: Geography helps explain trade because resources, climates, workers, technology, ports, and roads are not spread evenly, so different places produce, move, and buy different things.

questions.question: Explain one benefit and one challenge of globalization from the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: One benefit is that globalization can create jobs or give consumers more choices. One challenge is that it can cause pollution, unsafe working conditions, dependence on distant suppliers, or pressure on resources.

data.sourcePassage: A supply chain is the journey of a product from beginning to end. A cotton T-shirt may begin on a farm where cotton is grown. The cotton is processed, spun into thread, made into fabric, dyed, cut, and sewn. The shirt may then be packaged, loaded into a container, shipped across an ocean, unloaded at a port, moved to a warehouse, and sold in a store or online. The journey does not end when the customer buys it. The shirt may later be repaired, donated, reused, recycled, or thrown away. At every stage, geography matters. Cotton needs suitable climate and water. Factories need workers, energy, roads, and transport links. Ports need deep water, cranes, and connections to railways and highways.

questions.question: What is a supply chain?
questions.modelAnswer: A supply chain is the journey of a product from beginning to end.

questions.question: Which stage would most likely come before sewing a T-shirt?
options: Cotton is spun into thread and made into fabric
The shirt is bought by a customer
questions.modelAnswer: Cotton is spun into thread and made into fabric.

questions.question: Why do ports need connections to railways and highways?
questions.modelAnswer: Ports need railways and highways so goods unloaded from ships can move inland to warehouses, stores, factories, and consumers.

questions.question: Why is disposal or recycling part of a product's geography?
questions.modelAnswer: Disposal or recycling is part of geography because it happens in real places, uses transport and facilities, and can affect communities and environments through waste, pollution, or resource recovery.

data.sourcePassage: Cocoa beans grow best in warm, wet tropical regions near the Equator. A cocoa-growing region may have warm temperatures all year and rainfall in every month, with no freezing season. This means cocoa cannot grow well everywhere. Climate shapes where cocoa farms are located, and trade connects those farms to chocolate makers and consumers. Cocoa farmers harvest pods, remove the beans, ferment and dry them, and sell them into a supply chain. Chocolate bars are often made and sold by companies based in wealthier consumer markets. This can mean that farmers grow the raw material while more profit is earned elsewhere. Roads, ports, world prices, fair trade programs, and deforestation all affect whether the supply chain is fair and sustainable.

questions.question: What climate conditions help cocoa grow?
questions.modelAnswer: Cocoa grows best in warm, wet tropical conditions with no freezing season.

questions.question: Why would a cold, dry region struggle to grow cocoa?
options: Cocoa only grows in large cities
questions.modelAnswer: A cold, dry region would struggle because cocoa needs warmth and moisture.

questions.question: How does the cocoa example show interdependence?
questions.modelAnswer: The cocoa example shows interdependence because farmers, roads, ports, chocolate companies, consumers, and world prices are connected in one supply chain.

questions.question: What would make a chocolate supply chain more sustainable?
questions.modelAnswer: A more sustainable chocolate supply chain could pay farmers fairly, protect forests, improve roads and working conditions, reduce waste, and make company profits and sourcing more transparent.

data.sourcePassage: Transportation is central to global trade. Ships carry much of the world's long-distance trade because they can move huge amounts of goods at lower cost than airplanes. Standard metal containers changed trade because the same container can move from ship to train to truck. Ports need deep water, cranes, docks, warehouses, highways, and rail lines. Some trade locations are especially important because many goods pass through them. These are called chokepoints. The Panama Canal connects Atlantic and Pacific routes, the Suez Canal connects the Mediterranean Sea and Red Sea, and the Strait of Malacca links the Indian Ocean and Pacific Ocean. If a canal is blocked or a port closes after a storm, prices can rise and deliveries can slow in places far away.

questions.question: Why do ships carry much of the world's long-distance trade?
questions.modelAnswer: Ships can move huge amounts of goods across long distances at lower cost than airplanes.

questions.question: Which place is identified as a trade chokepoint?
questions.modelAnswer: The Panama Canal is a trade chokepoint.

questions.question: How did standard containers change global trade?
questions.modelAnswer: Standard containers made trade faster and cheaper because the same box can move efficiently between ships, trains, and trucks.

questions.question: Why can a port closure affect people far away?
questions.modelAnswer: A port closure can delay goods moving through supply chains, so stores, workers, businesses, and consumers in distant places may face shortages, higher prices, or delayed deliveries.

data.sourcePassage: Sustainable trade tries to balance economic, social, and environmental needs. Economic questions ask whether trade creates stable jobs and fair income. Social questions ask whether workers are safe, treated fairly, and able to have a voice in decisions. Environmental questions ask whether forests, soil, water, wildlife, and air are protected. Trade can create pollution from transport, water use in factories, deforestation for farming, and waste from packaging or discarded products. More sustainable choices can happen at many levels. Governments can create rules. Companies can improve supply chains and reduce waste. Communities can protect local resources. Consumers can buy durable products, repair items, reuse, recycle safely, thrift, and ask questions about how products are made.

questions.question: What three needs does sustainable trade try to balance?
questions.modelAnswer: Sustainable trade tries to balance economic, social, and environmental needs.

questions.question: Which choice best supports sustainability?
options: Repairing and reusing products when possible
Throwing away products after one use
questions.modelAnswer: Repairing and reusing products when possible supports sustainability.

questions.question: Give one environmental problem linked to trade from the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include pollution from transport, water use in factories, deforestation for farming, and waste from packaging or discarded products.

questions.question: Why does sustainability involve governments, companies, communities, and consumers?
questions.modelAnswer: Sustainability involves many groups because trade systems have many stages. Governments can make rules, companies control supply chains, communities manage local resources, and consumers influence demand and waste.
